title: "Chapter 17 checkpoint"
chapter: 17
checkpoint-quiz: true
subtitle: "Ten questions about streams, fields and trustworthy text processing."
---

Choose an answer before revealing its explanation. Revisit [pipes and grep](01-pipes-grep.html) or [awk and sed](02-awk-sed.html) if you can remember a command but cannot explain what it assumes about the data.

::: {.checkpoint title="1. Which stream enters a pipe?"}
In `analysis | wc -l`, what does `wc` normally receive?

- [x] The standard output of `analysis`

  Standard error remains separate unless explicitly redirected.
- [ ] Standard output and standard error, automatically merged

  A plain pipe does not merge the two streams. Combining diagnostics with data may corrupt downstream input.
- [ ] Only the last line printed by `analysis`

  The pipe transfers the output stream, not a single selected line.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="2. Seven lines, how many samples?"}
A newline-terminated TSV has one header and six sample records, each on one line. What does `wc -l < file.tsv` print?

- [ ] 6

  `wc` does not recognise and remove a header.
- [x] 7

  It counts newline characters, including the header's newline.
- [ ] The number of columns

  The `-l` option counts lines, not fields.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="3. Literal chemical notation"}
You want a literal substring search for `CC(=O)O`. Which choice makes that intent explicit?

- [x] `grep -F 'CC(=O)O' file`

  `-F` treats the pattern as fixed text. This is still a text search, not a molecular identity test.
- [ ] `grep -E 'CC(=O)O' file`

  In an extended regular expression, parentheses are grouping syntax rather than literal characters.
- [ ] Remove all punctuation before searching

  Punctuation is meaningful in molecular notation; removing it changes the text being searched.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="4. The empty search result"}
GNU `grep` prints no matches and returns exit status `1`. What does that mean?

- [ ] The file could not be opened

  A file-access error normally gives GNU grep status `2`, with a diagnostic on standard error.
- [x] The search completed without a match

  Expected absence is a different case from a broken search.
- [ ] Every line matched

  A successful match produces status `0`, not `1`.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="5. FASTA line counts"}
Why use `grep -c '^>'` to count records in the well-formed FASTA fixture?

- [ ] Every sequence occupies exactly one line

  A sequence may wrap over several lines; that is why total line counts are unsuitable.
- [x] Each record begins with one header line starting with `>`

  The count is useful, but it does not validate sequence content or identifier uniqueness.
- [ ] It counts nucleotides in each sequence

  `grep -c` counts matching lines, not sequence characters.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="6. Frequencies with uniq"}
Why does `cut -f 2 file.tsv | uniq -c` fail to count all occurrences of each condition reliably?

- [x] `uniq` combines adjacent repeats only, and the header may also be counted

  Skip the header, extract the field, sort the labels, then count repeats.
- [ ] `cut` always changes the labels

  `cut` selects the named field; it does not normally rewrite its contents.
- [ ] `uniq` cannot read from a pipe

  Reading standard input is a normal use of `uniq`.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="7. The tab separator"}
Why specify `awk -F '\t'` for this TSV rather than relying on the default separator?

- [ ] It makes arbitrary quoted CSV safe to read

  A tab separator does not implement CSV quoting rules or multiline fields.
- [x] It preserves the TSV's field boundaries, including empty fields

  Default whitespace splitting can collapse separators and shift field positions.
- [ ] It validates every scientific value automatically

  Separating fields and validating their values are different tasks.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="8. Before the numeric threshold"}
A field expected to hold reads in millions contains `NA`. What is the appropriate first step?

- [ ] Add zero and accept the result as a measured zero

  Missingness is not a measurement of zero. Silent coercion invents a value.
- [x] Validate the representation and apply an explicit missing-value policy

  Report or handle invalid records before thresholding or aggregation.
- [ ] Remove all letters from every column

  This would damage identifiers and labels while hiding the input problem.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="9. Where did the source go?"}
Why is `sed 's/A/B/' input.txt > input.txt` unsafe?

- [ ] sed cannot read plain text

  Processing text streams is sed's purpose.
- [x] The shell truncates the destination before sed can read the input

  Write to a different file and compare it with the preserved source.
- [ ] The pattern has too few characters

  Single-character patterns are valid. The problem is using the same input and output path.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="10. A quoted comma in CSV"}
A compound description is `"clear liquid, fruity odour"` inside a CSV field. Which tool choice respects that field?

- [ ] `awk -F ','`, because every comma separates columns

  The comma inside quotes belongs to one field. Splitting on all commas breaks the record.
- [ ] sed that deletes every comma inside the file

  That would destroy separators and alter the original content.
- [x] A CSV parser such as Python's csv module or pandas with appropriate options

  Use a parser that understands the format's quoting and record rules.
:::

Complete the [data-triage lab](labs/lab-17-data-triage.html), then carry these checks into [Bash automation](../ch18-bash-automation/index.html).
